slides.title: Chapter 8: Digital Signatures
slides.notes:
This is chapter 8 of Mastering Bitcoin, third edition. It explains what a digital signature proves and commits to, how Schnorr and ECDSA signatures work, and what has moved since the book went to print. The picture is the Bitcoin logo, which is in the public domain.

Every result was computed with the chapter's own Python library under Python 3.14.6. The answers of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0 were recorded once on a test network and are only read back in this deck, not run again. Each code slide has a twin in the chapter code tab of the course page, where you can change the listing and run it.

In chapter 7 a signature opened a lock. Here the signature itself is opened up.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.notes:
After the questions and the concept map, seven parts follow: the foundations of digital signatures, the signature hash flags called SIGHASH, Schnorr signatures, ECDSA signatures, randomness and signature size, signing in segregated witness, and what has changed since the book went to print. Each entry on the slide shows the slides where it lives, so you can jump straight to it.

The figures summarise the deck: fifty-one slides, twenty code examples that each end in a picture of the result, and three true stories.

The table on every divider slide repeats the route, so you always know which part you are reading. Chapter 7 is a good companion, because it shows where these signatures are checked.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.notes:
These seven questions are the chapter's own competency questions. Each has its answer on a slide, and the closing slide returns to them.

Use them as a self-test. The first asks what a verifier must have, and belongs to the foundations. The second concerns the SIGHASH flags and a bug in the flag called SINGLE. The third and fourth belong to Schnorr signatures: how a three-move proof becomes a 64-byte signature, and why adding keys is unsafe and how MuSig2 helps. The fifth concerns ECDSA, which can take two forms of one signature, and the difference between what consensus and policy accept. The sixth concerns the nonce and RFC 6979. The seventh asks what segregated witness changed in what is signed.

If a word is unfamiliar, the course page for chapter 8 has an entry for it.

slides.title: One chapter, seven parts
slides.notes:
The concept map shows the chapter as seven parts, with the number of key concepts and examples in each. Foundations has five concepts and three examples, SIGHASH eight and three, Schnorr signatures sixteen and five, ECDSA eight and three, randomness and signature size four and three, and segwit signing four and two. The last part, since the book went to print, has one example and the dates.

The counts show where the weight lies: Schnorr signatures carry the most concepts, because the book builds them up from a proof in several steps. The examples add up to twenty.

Every later slide belongs to one of these parts. The same map is on the course page, where you can filter it and open each concept.

slides.title: Foundations of digital signatures
slides.course_title: Anyone can check a signature; only the key owner can make it.
slides.notes:
Anyone can check a signature; only the key owner can make it. The signer holds the private key; everyone else checks with the public key.

This part has three themes. What a signature does: three inputs go in, a message, a public key and a signature, and a yes or no comes out. Arithmetic of the curve: two moduli are used, and scalars wrap at n while coordinates wrap at p. Signing a transaction: what is signed is not the transaction itself but a digest of it.

The table at the bottom marks where this part sits among the seven parts of the chapter.

slides.title: Foundations of digital signatures (1 of 2)
slides.notes:
Slide 7 makes these ideas concrete with a real signature and three checks.

A digital signature does three things at once: it shows that the key owner approved the message, it ties that approval to this exact message, and it can be checked by anybody. Chapter 7 showed signatures at work inside scripts; this chapter opens the signature itself. Real signatures in Bitcoin are 64 bytes (Schnorr) or about 70 bytes (ECDSA), as slides 24 and 32 measure.

slides.title: Three inputs, one answer
slides.notes:
The first box makes a secret key and a message, derives the public key that follows from the secret, and signs the message. The second box makes two altered inputs: the message with one bit flipped, and a different public key. The third box defines a small function, accepts, that asks the library to verify the signature for a given key and text, and tries three cases.

Changing the message or the key gives False.

This answers the first question of slide 3: a verifier needs the message, the public key and the signature, and then it can say yes or no. Example 1 lets you flip other bits.

Verification here is one call to the chapter's library, which is why the three cases stay short.

slides.title: Foundations of digital signatures (2 of 2)
slides.notes:
Slide 7 verified with the first idea, and slide 10 will show the second at work.

If you want to remember the pair: signing needs the secret, verifying needs only what is public.

Verifying needs only public data, which is why every node can do it. Elliptic curve points are the setting in which the discrete logarithm problem is used in Bitcoin. Remember the pair: signing needs the secret, verifying needs only what is public.

slides.title: Scalars wrap at n, coordinates at p
slides.course_title: Scalars wrap at n, coordinates at p
slides.notes:
Two moduli are used, and they are two clocks of different sizes. The group order n and the field prime p are different 256-bit numbers, which differ by a number of 129 bits.

The result table shows why this matters. The book says that everything is modulo p, but the response must be reduced modulo n.

A good rule is that the coordinates of points live modulo p, while secret keys, nonces and responses live modulo n. Example 2 lets you try other numbers.

Using the wrong modulus is a classic mistake in implementations of elliptic curve code.

slides.title: What is signed is a digest
slides.course_title: What is signed is a digest
slides.notes:
The signature covers a hash of the transaction, not the bytes themselves. The first box builds two identical transactions of two inputs and two outputs, and then raises one output amount of the second by one satoshi. The second box defines a function that computes the digest that is signed for the first input and shows its first twelve hexadecimal digits.

The result is the point of the slide. The same bytes give the same digest, 18bdeda48b41, twice.

Remember that any change to the covered bytes changes the digest. The SIGHASH flags of the next part decide which bytes are covered. Example 3 lets you change other fields.

The SIGHASH flags change which bytes feed this digest.

slides.title: Signature hash flags (SIGHASH)
slides.course_title: A flag chooses which parts of the transaction the signature covers.
slides.notes:
A flag chooses which parts of the transaction the signature covers. Part three is about the signature hash flags, called SIGHASH, which tell the verifier which fields of a transaction the signature commits to.

How flags are coded: a flag is one byte appended to the signature. Commitments by flag: each flag fixes some fields and leaves others open, so a signer can allow others to add inputs or change outputs. Known pitfalls: a flag called SINGLE signs the number one when no matching output exists, which slide 16 demonstrates.

Remember that a signature without a flag choice is a signature with the default, which commits to everything. The table at the bottom marks this part among the seven.

slides.title: Signature hash flags (SIGHASH) (1 of 2)
slides.notes:
Slide 13 shows how the flag is coded, and slide 14 completes the list.

In a script, the flag is stored as the last byte of the signature. Choosing a flag means choosing what the signer leaves open: SIGHASH_ALL leaves nothing open, and SIGHASH_NONE leaves every output open. Because the digest is made after the flag has chosen the covered fields, one transaction gives a different digest for each flag. Slide 13 shows how the flag is coded, and slide 14 completes the list.

slides.title: A flag is one byte
slides.notes:
A flag is one byte. The first box lists the three base flags, SIGHASH_ALL, SIGHASH_NONE and SIGHASH_SINGLE, which are the numbers 1, 2 and 3. The second box takes the modifier, SIGHASH_ANYONECANPAY, which is 128, the top bit of the byte. The third box adds the modifier to every base flag with the bitwise or operator and prints the result: 129, 130 and 131.

Because the modifier is a single high bit, it combines with every base flag. Six flag values result: three base flags, alone and with the modifier. These are the six values probed on slide 15.

To remember it, the low bits choose the outputs and the top bit chooses the inputs. Example 4 lets you print the values.

The vertical bar in Python combines the bits of two numbers, which is what makes the six values.

slides.title: Signature hash flags (SIGHASH) (2 of 2)
slides.notes:
Slide 15 measures what each flag commits to, and slide 16 shows a bug in SINGLE.

The hash types combine: ANYONECANPAY can be added to ALL, NONE or SINGLE. Taproot's zero byte is only a shorthand, so a default signature carries no flag byte at all and stays at 64 bytes. Slide 15 measures what each flag commits to, and slide 16 shows a bug in SINGLE. The text of BIP118 holds the details of the proposal.

slides.title: What each flag commits to
slides.notes:
The second box probes five parts of a transaction. For each flag it changes one field at a time and checks whether the digest moves; a field that moves the digest is covered by the flag. The third box counts the covered fields for each flag.

The field pattern in the result text, such as ....Y., marks which fields are covered.

Only plain ALL covers every probed field, including the sequence numbers of the other inputs. The other flags leave something open for others to change. Example 5 lets you probe other fields.

The sequence numbers of the other inputs are among the probed fields.

slides.title: SINGLE with no matching output
slides.notes:
The first box builds a transaction with three inputs and only one output. Input 0 has an output, but inputs 1 and 2 have none. For those two, the legacy algorithm signs the constant number one instead of a real digest. That is why their digests begin with 01000000, the number one written in bytes, and why the third box prints False for input 0 and True for the other two.

A digest that is always the number one can be reused on any transaction, so a signature made this way commits to nothing. The book does not mention this bug. The slides on segwit signing show how the newer algorithm changed what is signed. Example 6 lets you add outputs.

A digest that begins with 01000000 is the number one written in bytes.

slides.title: Schnorr signatures
slides.course_title: Schnorr signatures can be added together.
slides.notes:
Schnorr signatures can be added together. This part builds up the scheme in four steps.

Proof to signature shows how a three-move proof becomes a signature by hashing. The BIP340 format covers the fixed sizes, the x-only keys and the tagged hashes of the Bitcoin version. Aggregating keys shows that keys and signatures add up, with one trap that slide 26 demonstrates. Threshold sharing shows that any two of three key holders can sign.

Chapter 7 told why this matters: taproot spends with a key path, one signature that hides how many people signed. This part explains that signature.

slides.title: Schnorr signatures: key concepts (1 of 4)
slides.notes:
Slides 19 and 21 build up the equation.

The three scriptless ideas share one fact: the chain only ever sees one ordinary key and one ordinary signature. The group structure is kept off the chain, which makes such spends smaller and more private than the scripted multisignature of chapter 7. Slides 19 and 21 build up the equation step by step. A Schnorr signature is made of the point R and the number s, so its size never varies, unlike the DER signatures of ECDSA.

slides.title: The protocol with whole numbers
slides.notes:
The book first explains Schnorr with whole numbers. The toy run uses the secret x = 3, the generator G = 5, the nonce k = 7 and the challenge e = 11. The point of a number is just five times it, so the public key xG is 15 and the commitment kG is 35.

The verifier checks that sG = kG + e xG, which is 200 = 35 + 165, and the check holds.

The danger is on the last line: dividing the public number xG by G returns the secret 3. With points on a curve that division is impossible, which is why points are used. Example 7 lets you change the numbers.

Toy numbers make the arithmetic visible; real keys are 256-bit numbers on a curve.

slides.title: Schnorr signatures: key concepts (2 of 4)
slides.notes:
Slide 21 shows it.

Remember the order of the ideas: proof, challenge, hash, signature.

Interactive means that a prover talks to a verifier; Fiat-Shamir removes the conversation by letting a hash of the message play the verifier. Keep the order of the ideas in mind: proof, challenge, hash, signature. An x-only key leaves out whether y is even or odd by always assuming an even y, as slide 24 measures in bytes. BIP340 fixes the exact hashing, so wallets from different makers produce signatures that every node can check. Slide 21 shows the Fiat-Shamir step.

slides.title: From identity proof to signature
slides.notes:
A prover with the secret x publishes the point X = xG, picks a nonce k, sends the point R = kG and receives a challenge e. The prover answers with s = k + e x, and the verifier checks that sG equals R + eX. The honest response is accepted, and the response plus one is rejected.

The third box applies the Fiat-Shamir idea: the hash of the message plays the examiner, so no examiner has to be online. 

The numbers are small toy values for readability. Slide 19 showed the same equation with whole numbers, and example 8 lets you change the message.

The toy values keep the arithmetic readable; the structure is the one used with real keys.

slides.title: The signature that was patented for two decades
slides.course_title: The signature that was patented for two decades
slides.notes: Claus-Peter Schnorr's signature scheme was patented in the United States as patent 4,995,082, published on 19 February 1991. The patent kept the scheme out of open standards, so ECDSA was the only signature that Bitcoin knew until 2021. The term of the patent was the longer of 17 years from the grant and 20 years from the filing, so it ended on 23 February 2010. BIP340 is Schnorr's scheme fitted to the curve secp256k1, and it went live with taproot, thirty years after the paper. The portrait shows Claus-Peter Schnorr at Oberwolfach in 1986, by Konrad Jacobs, MFO, CC BY-SA 2.0 de. The patent itself is linked on the slide.

slides.title: Schnorr signatures: key concepts (3 of 4)
slides.notes: Linearity makes aggregation possible, batch verification saves work, key prefixing binds the signature to its key and the scriptless form hides the group. Key prefixing is part of the design of BIP340. In the scriptless form the count of signers is hidden inside the keys, and slides 25 and 26 show the danger that comes with it. Compare chapter 7, slide 21, where OP_CHECKMULTISIG counted the signers in a visible script.

slides.title: A fixed size: 64 bytes
slides.notes:
BIP340 keys are 32 bytes and signatures are 64 bytes. The first box makes a secret key and the hash of a message. The second box makes the BIP340 objects, an x-only public key and a 64-byte signature, and for comparison the ECDSA objects: the compressed public key and the signature of the same key. The third box verifies the Schnorr signature and lists the four sizes.

DER signatures vary in size, as slide 41 shows.

Fixed sizes make fees easier to estimate and parsing simpler. Example 9 lets you sign other messages.

The x-only key is one byte shorter because the sign of the y coordinate is not stored.

slides.title: Schnorr signatures: key concepts (4 of 4)
slides.notes: Shamir secret sharing was published by Adi Shamir in 1979, long before Bitcoin. Two points fix a line, so any two shares recover the secret, while a single share fits every possible line. MuSig2 and Shamir sharing solve different problems: the first protects against a dishonest signer, the second against lost shares. Both ideas let a group act as one key, which is the goal of the scriptless forms on slide 23. Slide 26 shows the attack, and slide 27 shows the sharing.

slides.title: A key that cancels another key
slides.course_title: A key that cancels another key
slides.notes:
The table compares two ways of combining keys. Against a plain sum of keys, Bob can sign alone: yes, valid. Against MuSig2 weighted keys he cannot.

The plain sum of the two keys is then a key that he alone controls, so he signs for both of them. The second box runs the same attempt against MuSig2. Every key is weighted by a hash of all the keys, so Bob cannot choose a key that cancels Alice's, and the attack fails.

Remember that adding public keys is not enough. The group must bind each key to the whole group, which is what the weights do. Example 10 lets you change the attacker's numbers.

A naive key sum fails because the attacker chooses his key after seeing hers.

slides.title: Any two of three shares
slides.notes:
Any two points determine the line and therefore the secret, so every pair of shares gives 31337.

The second box combines every pair, and the third box tries one share alone. A single share is consistent with every possible secret, so fewer shares than the threshold reveal nothing, and the threshold reveals everything.

This is the idea behind the scriptless threshold signatures of slide 25. Compare slide 26: there the danger was a dishonest signer, here the danger is losing shares. Example 11 lets you change the secret.

The scheme tolerates lost shares: any two of the three still work.

slides.title: ECDSA signatures
slides.course_title: ECDSA is the older scheme, with a messier signature format and two valid shapes.
slides.notes: ECDSA is the older scheme, with a messier signature format and two valid shapes. It was Bitcoin's only signature from 2009 until Schnorr joined it in 2021, so the signatures in older transactions are all of this kind. The part has three themes. The ECDSA equations: two formulas, and two valid values of s. DER serialization: a signature is written as nested length-prefixed fields. Compare this part with the Schnorr part before it, whose equation is simpler. The differences you meet here are the price of the older design.

slides.title: ECDSA signatures: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.notes:
Slide 30 follows the algorithm with chosen numbers, and slide 32 takes a real DER signature apart.

The first release of Bitcoin used ECDSA on the secp256k1 curve, and Schnorr signatures joined it with the taproot upgrade. The inversion in the ECDSA formula is what makes it messier than Schnorr's s = k + e x. Slide 30 follows the algorithm with chosen numbers, and slide 32 takes a real DER signature apart. DER, the byte layout of the pair R and s, is met again on slide 31.

slides.title: ECDSA with the book's formulas
slides.notes:
The first box takes toy values: the key x = 0x1234, the message hash h = 0x5678 and the nonce k = 0x9abc. It signs with that explicit nonce, where R is the x coordinate of the point kG and s follows from the book's formula. The second box defines verification: the library rebuilds a point K from s, R and the public key and compares it with R. The third box tries both s and n minus s.

If s verifies, so does n minus s, so the signature has two forms.

This is the malleability of slide 31 and the policy of slide 34. Example 12 lets you try other nonces.

The chosen nonce is for teaching; real signers derive it as slide 40 shows.

slides.title: ECDSA signatures: key concepts (2 of 2)
slides.notes: Malleability matters because it could change the identifier of a transaction, as chapter 7 explained for spends without a witness. Slide 34 compares consensus with policy. The low-S rule is a relay policy and not a consensus rule, as slide 34 shows, so a wallet that always produces the low form keeps its transactions relayable. The four cards belong together: two forms exist, a relay rule picks one, and DER is how the chosen pair is written down.

slides.title: Nine elements in 71 bytes
slides.notes:
The library splits it into the nine elements that the book lists and counts the bytes of each. R and s take 32 bytes each, and the other seven elements take one byte each: the sequence marker, the total length, the integer marker and length of R, the integer marker and length of s, and the hash type.

When the top bit of R is set, a zero byte is added in front and R takes 33 bytes, as slides 33 and 41 show. Example 13 lets you cut other signatures.

A DER signature begins with 0x30, the marker of a sequence.

slides.title: The signature on the page is a real payment
slides.course_title: The signature on the page is a real payment
slides.notes:
The long hexadecimal signature that the book dissects in its DER section is a real signature from a mined payment. It was mined in block 277,316 on 27 December 2013 at 23:11:54 UTC. A real example can be checked: the chapter recomputes it, and signature, key and transaction agree.

Its R has 33 bytes because its top bit is set, which is the case of slide 32. Its S is already the low form, so a node would still relay it today, as slide 34 explains.

No photograph exists, because nobody knows who sent this payment. The Bitcoin logo, by Grayliptrot and in the public domain on Wikimedia Commons, stands in. The mempool.space link on the slide opens the transaction itself.

slides.title: Valid for miners, refused by nodes
slides.course_title: Valid for miners, refused by nodes
slides.notes: The first box takes one low-S signature and builds its twin by replacing s with n minus s. The second box defines two checks: is_valid asks whether the signature verifies, and is_low_s asks whether it has the low-S form. The third box applies both checks to the two signatures. The low-S form is valid and relayed. The high-S twin is valid but not relayed. Miners accept both, because both are valid. Nodes relay only the low-S form, which is a stricter house rule. Remember that valid is not the same as relayed. Consensus is the law, and policy is a stricter house rule. Example 14 lets you try other messages. Valid and relayed are two different questions: the first belongs to consensus, the second to policy.

slides.title: Policy or consensus?
slides.notes: Consensus decides what is valid: every node must agree on it, or the chain splits, and a change needs a soft or a hard fork. Policy decides what is relayed: each node may choose its own rules, and a change needs only a new release. High S is policy, so miners accept such a signature but ordinary nodes do not relay it. Strict DER became consensus in 2015. Keeping the two apart explains why a transaction can be valid and yet never reach a miner through ordinary nodes. Remember the pair: consensus is about validity, policy is about relay.

slides.title: Randomness and signature size
slides.course_title: Randomness and signature size: key concepts
slides.notes:
Slide 38 computes the leak, slide 39 tells a real incident, and slide 40 shows the cure.

A weak or repeated nonce has cost real users their funds, as slide 39 tells. RFC 6979 is the cure of slide 40: when nothing random is drawn, there is nothing to repeat. Slide 38 computes the leak, and slide 40 shows the cure. The nonce is the weakest point of the scheme in practice: the mathematics is sound, but a bad random number generator breaks it.

slides.title: One nonce, two signatures, no secret
slides.course_title: One nonce, two signatures, no secret
slides.notes:
Because both signatures share R, anyone can see that the nonce was reused. Two equations with two unknowns remain: subtracting one equation from the other and dividing gives the nonce, and from the nonce the private key falls out. The values are small toy numbers.

The third box signs the second message with a fresh nonce. Then R differs and nothing leaks. The table shows the observations: the same R in both signatures, the private key recovered, and the nonce recovered.

Slide 39 tells how this attack became possible in 2013. Example 15 lets you change the nonce.

Subtracting the two equations removes the secret key from the difference, which is why the nonce can be solved first.

slides.title: When the phone's random numbers were not random
slides.course_title: When the phone's random numbers were not random
slides.notes:
On 11 August 2013 Bitcoin.org warned that the random number generator of Android was weak, and that wallets built on it could be robbed. A weak generator can repeat or leak a nonce, and a repeated nonce hands over the private key, as slide 38 computed.

Alex Klyubin of Google explained the flaw on 14 August, and Bitcoin Wallet and other wallets shipped updates. RFC 6979 derives the nonce from the key and the message, which is why Bitcoin Core no longer needs a good generator for it.

The Android robot, by Google Inc. and designed by Irina Blok, CC BY 3.0, stands in for the platform and does not show the incident. The Bitcoin.org alert is linked on the slide.

slides.title: The nonce derived from the key
slides.course_title: The nonce derived from the key
slides.notes:
The second box derives one for another message, and the third box repeats the first derivation and the signature itself.

The same key and message always give the same nonce, 0x1f8bce02bda8 at the start, and so the same signature. Another message gives another nonce, which starts with 0x80fb94370ee8.

Nothing random is drawn, so there is nothing to repeat by accident. Two different messages never share a nonce, so the attack of slide 38 has nothing to work on. The derivation uses HMAC, a keyed hash. Example 16 lets you derive nonces for other messages.

HMAC is a hash that takes a secret key as an extra input.

slides.title: About half are one byte longer
slides.course_title: About half are one byte longer
slides.notes:
The first box signs 200 different messages with one key. The second box collects the length of every signature. The third box counts the lengths: about half of the signatures are 70 bytes long and about half are 71.

A 33-byte R, needed when its top bit is set, makes the signature one byte longer. It is the zero byte of slide 32.

One byte hardly matters for one signature, but it adds up over many. Compare slide 24, where a Schnorr signature always takes 64 bytes, so there is no length to optimise. Example 17 lets you sign more messages.

Signing again until R is small costs a little time and saves a byte on each signature.

slides.title: Segwit signing
slides.notes: Segregated witness changed what is hashed when a transaction is signed. The new signing algorithm, written in BIP143, hashes the shared parts of the transaction once and also covers the amount being spent. This part has three themes. The cost of hashing compares the old and the new method by counting bytes. The commitment to amounts shows why the amount is now part of the signature. Taproot signing shows that a taproot spend carries one 64-byte signature. Remember that the amount in the digest protects signers who cannot see the earlier transaction.
slides.course_title: Segwit signing: the amount is covered

slides.title: Quadratic hashing
slides.notes: The old signing algorithm hashes almost the whole transaction again for every input. BIP143 hashes the shared parts once, so its cost grows in step with the number of inputs. The ratio of the two grows with the number of inputs, which the chart shows by counting bytes. Quadratic means that the cost grows with the square of the number of inputs, and linear means that it grows in proportion. It is example 18 in the chapter code tab of the course page, where you can change the number of inputs.

slides.title: BIP143 signs the amount
slides.notes:
The first box makes one input and the script of a pay-to-key-hash coin, which stays the same: OP_DUP, OP_HASH160, a 20-byte hash, OP_EQUALVERIFY and OP_CHECKSIG. The second box defines a function that computes the BIP143 digest for a given amount. The third box computes it for 5,000 satoshis twice and for 5,001, and the legacy digest for comparison.

The BIP143 digest for 5,000 is 3d02f61132ca both times, and for 5,001 it is 89c355aa699d. The legacy digest, 0d29c866d5f0, has no amount in it, so a wallet could be told any value.

With the amount signed, a wallet can no longer be lied to about the value. Compare chapter 7, slide 39. Example 19 lets you change the amount.

The amount in the digest protects offline signers such as hardware wallets, which cannot see the earlier transaction themselves.

slides.title: Since the book went to print
slides.course_title: A statement in the book is a snapshot of its print date.
slides.notes:
A statement in the book is a snapshot of its print date. This part marks what in the book may have changed.

Standards status: proposals move from draft to deployed. Library support: Bitcoin Core and its library add features after print. History and dates: the patent, the first spend and the activation. The evidence trail: every claim is tied to a saved source or to a run.

When you read the book, treat a statement of status as a snapshot of its print date and check it against the sources listed on slide 50.

slides.title: Dates behind the patent and taproot
slides.course_title: Dates behind the patent and taproot
slides.notes:
The term is the longer of 17 years from the grant, which is 2008-02-19, and 20 years from the filing, which is 2010-02-23.

The third box counts the days from the genesis block, 3 January 2009, to the activation of taproot on 14 November 2021, which is 4,698 days. The patent ended in 2010, and taproot came eleven years later.

The code uses the date type of Python, which does the calendar arithmetic. Compare slide 22, which told the story of the patent. Example 20 lets you change the dates.

Subtracting two Python dates gives a time span whose days attribute is the count.

slides.title: Status of the BIPs the chapter names
slides.course_title: Status of the BIPs the chapter names
slides.notes:
The chapter names thirteen BIPs, and their status was read from the saved BIP index. Deployed: 66, 143, 327, 340, 341 and 342. Drafts: 118, 361, 390 and 461. Complete: 54 and 373. Closed: 146.

A deployed proposal is in use on the network. A draft is still being worked on and may change. The counts were made from the saved index in deck 1.1.0 under Python 3.14.6.

A status can change after print, so check the index of the BIPs repository when you rely on it. Two examples from this chapter: BIP118 on slide 14 is a proposal, and BIP327 on slide 25 is deployed in the sense of this index.

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.notes:
The five lines summarise the chapter, one line for each part, and each can be proved from its slides.

A signature is checked from message, public key and signature, scalars wrap at n, and the digest is what is signed. A SIGHASH flag chooses what is signed, and SINGLE with no matching output signs the number one. Schnorr turns a three-move proof into 64 bytes, keys add up safely only with MuSig2, and shares give thresholds. ECDSA has two forms of s and a nested byte layout, and a reused nonce leaks the key, which RFC 6979 prevents. Segwit hashes less and signs the amount, policy is stricter than consensus, and standards moved after print.

If a line feels unproven, the code slide of its part carries the receipt.

slides.title: Where to go from here
slides.notes:
Everything on this slide is free to read or watch, and every entry was opened on 2026-10-23 and is a live link in the file. The groups form a path. Read starts with the BIP340 specification, which has reference code and test vectors, the chapter's source on GitHub and the Bitcoin Wiki article on OP_CHECKSIG.

Standards and papers are the authoritative texts: BIP327 for MuSig2, RFC 6979 for the nonce, and Schnorr's paper of 1991. Watch has the MIT course Blockchain and Money, and the Optech workshop on Schnorr and taproot. Community has the Optech newsletters, the Delving Bitcoin forum, and the bitcoin-dev mailing list, where BIPs and soft forks are first proposed.

A good order is the workshop first, then BIP340 beside the chapter.

slides.title: What you should now be able to say
slides.course_title: And where each claim gets its proof
slides.notes:
These four statements are what you should be able to say after the chapter: what a verifier needs, what each SIGHASH flag commits to, how Schnorr, MuSig2 and ECDSA signatures work, and why the nonce matters and how policy differs from consensus.

Each is carried by a computation that ran on a slide of this deck, and slide 49 lists where. A statement you cannot yet say in your own words sends you back to that slide, and the questions on slide 3 are a good test.

The course page for chapter 8 has every word behind the slides, the stories with their sources and the question bank. Bring remaining questions to your instructor, and use the community links on slide 50.
